summary: During major disasters, optical satellites are rendered blind by storm clouds, rain, and darkness. SARScope overcomes this barrier by harnessing NASA–ISRO SAR (NISAR) L-band dual-polarisation radar. Using an edge-optimised machine learning pipeline (random forest + multi-temporal baseline subtraction), SARScope detects surface water dynamics, flood spread, and saturated soil with a validated 0.937 F1-score. Crucially, it translates raw radar science into action—automatically calculating tactical waypoint corridors and exporting flight-ready rescue packages (.kml, .geojson) for first-responder drone teams within minutes.
details:
SARScope: Seeing Through the Storm

What it does and how it works

When a cyclone hits or the monsoon turns violent, the satellites most of us rely on go blind. Optical sensors can’t see through thick cloud, and they can’t see at night. That’s exactly when rescue teams need to know where the water is.

SARScope fills that gap using radar from NISAR, the joint NASA–ISRO satellite. Its L-band radar passes straight through clouds and darkness, and it picks up how the ground scatters microwaves back to space. Water, wet soil, and dry land all reflect differently. We feed those signals (backscatter strength, how well the surface conducts radar, and surface texture) into a lightweight machine learning pipeline built on a Random Forest, and we compare new images against a pre-flood baseline. The result is a clear picture of where water is spreading, how fast, and where it’s still standing after the storm passes, all in near real time.

Why it matters

No blind spots when it counts. Monsoons, hurricanes, and nighttime floods are when optical satellites fail. SARScope keeps working.

From satellite data to a rescue route. Flood maps are only useful if someone can act on them. SARScope turns detected flood boundaries into drone flight corridors, exported as .kml, .geojson, or .csv, so rescue teams can launch UAVs toward stranded people without any manual conversion.

One complete picture. We combine NISAR radar with NASA LANCE optical data (MODIS and VIIRS) and SMAP soil moisture, producing a full disaster briefing within minutes of a satellite pass.

Under the hood

  • Analytics and ML: Python, Scikit-Learn, GDAL, Rasterio, NumPy, and SciPy, handling multi-temporal differencing, spatial holdout validation, and GCOV HDF5 subsetting.
  • Backend: FastAPI, Uvicorn, and Pydantic. Instead of downloading multi-gigabyte files, we use HTTP range requests to pull only the bytes covering the area of interest straight from NASA’s servers.
  • Frontend: React 19, Vite, and MapLibre GL JS, with 3D terrain (1.5× exaggeration, using AWS Terrarium elevation data) and Lucide icons.
